name: Injection Molding

claims.claim_text: A part almost never ejects cleanly from a new tool on the first attempt; on one design the part jammed so hard that the ejector pins sheared off before the plastic gave way.
claims.quote_verbatim: we broke the injection pins or the eject pins off because it jammed up so hard
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: The scarce skill in a molded product is the toolmaker rather than the part designer: early units can be machined from solid aluminium at any cost, but production without a senior mold designer produces exactly the ejection failures that stop a line.
claims.quote_verbatim: you really have to find that unicorn, the person that knows how to make the tools
claims.speaker: Jeri Ellsworth
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Jeri Ellsworth - Intense Illusion Introduction

claims.claim_text: Draft angle exists because a molded wall cannot be perpendicular: without taper the part tears against the tool as it is pulled, so a nominally square feature comes out slightly trapezoidal.
claims.quote_verbatim: you can't have straight 90 degree angles. Cause when you pull the mold out, then you'll start tearing at the, the, the, the plastic you just molded
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ryan O'Hara - Keyed, Kerfed Kapton

claims.claim_text: The process itself is pellets melted and driven forward by a screw, then forced under hundreds of tons of clamping pressure into a mold machined to very tight precision or cut by electrical discharge machining.
claims.quote_verbatim: plastic pellets are heated up and then they're pushed through a screw, which is a way of transferring torque
claims.speaker: John Saunders

claims.claim_text: A production tool for a part as small as a plastic brick was estimated at tens of thousands to a couple of hundred thousand dollars in the United States.
claims.quote_verbatim: would probably be, I'm going to just take a guess, $40,000 to $200,000
claims.speaker: John Saunders

claims.claim_text: Tooling quotes vary by orders of magnitude with where the tool is cut, with non-recurring engineering for a molded part in China quoted around five hundred dollars.
claims.quote_verbatim: In China, you can get injection molded NRE cost of like 500 bucks
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: At quantities around a thousand parts nobody is using true high-pressure molding; the work is done on bench presses, by machining, by printing or by low-pressure molding, all of which avoid the multi-hundred-ton machine entirely.
claims.quote_verbatim: it's still not the case that people who have a thousand of something are doing it with what we would consider injection molding
claims.speaker: John Saunders

claims.claim_text: There is a spectrum of molding processes below full injection molding, usable for test parts or short production runs.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's a ton of ways to mold things that are not under the multi hundred ton pressure of injection molding
claims.speaker: John Saunders

claims.claim_text: The plastic brick is a rare molded product whose outer walls really are square and perpendicular, achieved by putting all the draft on the inside surface of the part.
claims.quote_verbatim: they actually run the draft through the ID of a Lego
claims.speaker: John Saunders

claims.claim_text: Parts leave the tool carrying enough electrostatic charge to bounce back out of the collection bin, striking the side to discharge before they will settle.
claims.quote_verbatim: these parts coming out have such a high static electricity charge that when they fall into the bucket, they're repelled back up
claims.speaker: Eric Van Wyk
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric VanWyk - Meiotic Mountenance Mooshimeter

claims.claim_text: Design-for-manufacture guidance for molding is tiered by tooling budget: cheap tools come with one set of draft-angle and wall rules, expensive tools relax them, and the highest tier is capability effectively unavailable to anyone else.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you're running really cheap molds, you can have this draft angle and a bunch of guidelines. If you're expensive, you can do this
claims.speaker: Eric Van Wyk
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric VanWyk - Meiotic Mountenance Mooshimeter

claims.claim_text: Around five thousand units is the rough crossover where prototype-style processes stop being the cheaper route and tooling starts to pay, though the type of mold still matters below the high-volume threshold.
claims.quote_verbatim: So 5,000 is where things are looking pretty good
claims.speaker: Eric Van Wyk
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric VanWyk - Meiotic Mountenance Mooshimeter

claims.claim_text: A correction that adds material to the part is cheap because it only means cutting more steel out of the tool, which is why designing so that fixes go in that direction keeps changes quick.
claims.quote_verbatim: fortunately it was just adding plastic so that it was a pretty quick remachining
claims.speaker: Eric Van Wyk
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Eric VanWyk - Meiotic Mountenance Mooshimeter

claims.claim_text: A field failure in a mechanical switch traced back to dimensional variation in the molded parts, despite two years of prototypes on what was nominally the same tool never showing it.
claims.quote_verbatim: it turns out that it was just a tolerance thing in the injection molded parts

claims.claim_text: The same tool does not give the same part: shot speed and melt temperature are all adjustable, so pre-production and production runs can differ, and a defect affecting a small percentage is invisible in a fifty-unit build and obvious at five hundred or a thousand.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you shoot plastic faster or hotter or colder

claims.claim_text: Plastic shrinks as it leaves the tool, so the drawing carries a shrinkage allowance rather than the measured dimension; re-baselining the drawing to the shrunk parts as a factory requested would make the next tool cut to the shrunk size and shrink again from there, ratcheting the part smaller with every generation.
claims.quote_verbatim: now whenever I leave the company and someone else needs to go and get another mold made, they're now going to make the mold for the new shrunk size. And it's going to shrink again
claims.speaker: Parker Dillman

claims.claim_text: Worn tools show themselves as flash where the mold halves no longer close cleanly, producing a rim of excess material around the parting line.
claims.quote_verbatim: some of them were just so poorly molded that they'd have lots of flash
claims.speaker: Fran Blanche

claims.claim_text: Colour contamination from an incompletely purged machine carries the previous run into the next, which forced hand inspection of every piece in a thousand-unit order of light-coloured parts.
claims.quote_verbatim: I'd order white knobs, but they're filled with flecks of black and blue and red because they didn't clean out the machine completely
claims.speaker: Fran Blanche

claims.claim_text: Fixing a board outline across successive product versions lets one enclosure tool be amortised over several generations instead of being a single-product cost.
claims.quote_verbatim: if Bus Pirate version 4, 5, 6, 7 all use that same profile, then our investment in injection mold is, you know, we can drag that out over some time
claims.speaker: Ian Lesnet
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Ian Lesnet - Bus Buccaneer Builder

claims.claim_text: At a build of well under two thousand units a custom hard tool for an enclosure is not the right call, with a soft mold the sensible alternative.
claims.quote_verbatim: that's not a huge volume. You know, you wouldn't go injection molding a custom enclosure for it
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: The threshold is not absolute: one small-volume product ran a molded case while being built in batches of a thousand at a time.
claims.quote_verbatim: I already have one product with an injection molded case that I'm only manufacturing in quantities of 1,000 at a time
claims.speaker: Michael Ossmann
claims.episode_title: Interview with Michael Ossmann - Gifted Grimgribber Grokker

claims.claim_text: Regulated products need a certifiable unit long before mass tooling exists, which is what soft tooling is for: it costs far less and wears out much sooner, but yields fully functional parts good enough to pass regulatory testing and to look like the real product.
claims.quote_verbatim: you pay a lot less money for soft tools that burn out a lot sooner but that nonetheless allow you to produce pretty reasonable quality products
claims.speaker: Eric Ries
claims.episode_title: Interview with Eric Ries - Transorted Testing Tachydidaxy

claims.claim_text: Tooling lead time set the iteration rate of an entire industry: appliance models appeared every five to seven years because design plus tooling took that long, and the process rules were built around that pace even for products that would sell in the thousands.
claims.quote_verbatim: tended to come out like every five to seven years because it took a long time to design and you need to build money and all this tooling
claims.speaker: Eric Ries
claims.episode_title: Interview with Eric Ries - Transorted Testing Tachydidaxy

claims.claim_text: Tooling a single small proprietary connector plug cost around eighteen thousand dollars, which is the scale of commitment behind even a trivial-looking molded part.
claims.quote_verbatim: That was a cool $18,000 you just spent, huh?
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Adam Wolf - Brick & Board Biuners

claims.claim_text: Toy companies employ dedicated costing engineers who estimate a part by weighing the plastic, pricing the raw resin and adding the molding cycle time for that specific geometry.
claims.quote_verbatim: They'll actually weigh every piece of plastic and then factor in the cost of the raw resin and the, and the injection molding cycling time for that part
claims.speaker: Julia Truchsess

claims.claim_text: Past the tooling cost the marginal cost of molded plastic is close to nothing: on an inexpensive vacuum cleaner the copper motor windings are the expensive content while the entire plastic body is around a dollar on a million-shot tool.
claims.quote_verbatim: once you get past that, that mold cost, it's so incredibly cheap
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Boeing, PCBs & Startups - Awful Airplane Aeration

claims.claim_text: No additive process competes with molding on throughput, because the cycle is simply heating plastic and shooting it into a tool.
claims.quote_verbatim: you're never going to go faster than an injection mold
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: CAD courses and cross platform creation - Printing Propaedeutic Patterns

claims.claim_text: A crowdfunded product that printed all its enclosures ended up running a room of printers continuously to keep up, which its maker afterwards called a mistake.
claims.quote_verbatim: they had to have, you know, a room full of 3D printers just running 24-7
claims.speaker: Dave Jones
claims.episode_title: CAD courses and cross platform creation - Printing Propaedeutic Patterns

claims.claim_text: Molding penalises variation in a way printing does not: each variant of a design needs its own tool, so an engineer's time spent modifying a model is trivial next to the cost of the mold it implies.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you would like to make a variation of your design, then you will pay a lot of money for the new mold
claims.speaker: Claire Wolf

claims.claim_text: A geometry a printer will happily produce can be impossible to mold, so proving a feature on a printed prototype says nothing about whether it can be made in volume.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you have an actual mold, if you're trying to do any kind of volume, there's no way that's going to work
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: FPGA, Xess, 32 Bit - Quirky Qualitative Questions

claims.claim_text: Prototype shots looking good is not evidence that a part is production-ready: across tens of thousands of shots the tool wears and the plastic sags, and cosmetic acceptance shifts once someone is judging finished product.
claims.quote_verbatim: It looked good as a prototype, but this isn't good when you're going to be shooting 50,000, you know, injection molded plastic pieces. Because over time, the moldwares and the plastic sags

claims.claim_text: An off-the-shelf enclosure is frequently good enough for the look and feel of a product, and going fully custom adds certification work on top of tooling, which is what pushes people back toward standard parts on the next design.
claims.quote_verbatim: You don't have to gild the lily and go completely injection molded and everything else

claims.claim_text: Custom tooling buys freedom at volume, including parts such as bespoke battery form factors that cannot be bought from a catalogue, but it also removes every fallback: with a custom molded part there is no equivalent of buying a project box when the tool fails.
claims.quote_verbatim: custom is great until you realize that then you, you are the supply chain. There is no backup
claims.speaker: Jeff Keyzer

claims.claim_text: Die casting is the same process with metal: material injected at high pressure, typically a hundred or two hundred degrees above its melting point so it reaches every crevice before solidifying.
claims.quote_verbatim: It's basically just like injection molding, but they inject metal at high pressure instead of plastic
claims.speaker: David Kronstein

claims.claim_text: Pushing complexity into the tool is usually the right trade: features such as a battery retention detail need slides and draws that make the mold more expensive, but the extra plastic per shot costs essentially nothing.
claims.quote_verbatim: the mold will be a little bit more expensive. It might have different slides and draws
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: Custom mechanical parts should be designed so that a prototype can be machined or printed even when production will be die cast or molded, rather than discovering at the end that the production geometry cannot be prototyped.
claims.quote_verbatim: make sure you design it so that it is machinable for in the case of metal right so it's machinable as a prototype or it's 3d printable
claims.speaker: Dave Jones

claims.claim_text: A hands-on manufacturing course took students from solid modelling through having tooling cut, and treated surface finish and resin choice between ABS and polycarbonate as decisions the designer makes, alongside techniques such as in-mold lamination.
claims.quote_verbatim: They had to choose their own finish
claims.speaker: Akiba

claims.claim_text: Published design-for-manufacture courses cover molding alongside die casting, rotational molding, factory selection, managing cost against quality and schedule, and waterproofing, with the molding module alone running to fifty or sixty slides.
claims.quote_verbatim: they cover everything from injection molding, die casting, roll to molding, how to pick a factory, how to manage cost quality and schedule, how to waterproof something
claims.speaker: Scott Miller

claims.claim_text: The recurring pattern is that a factory reviewing a finished design finds savings that could have been designed in from the start, which is the argument for pulling manufacturing knowledge earlier into the process.
claims.quote_verbatim: you would have saved five bucks or whatever
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Teardowns are a way to learn molding, because a part's shape carries the evidence of how it was made: a face is angled purely so the part will release reliably from the tool.
claims.quote_verbatim: the way a part is shaped and the fact that it's angled because it's the only way they can get it out of the mold
claims.speaker: John Day

claims.claim_text: The fastest route to learning mold design is having someone experienced critique your model, where the first finding is usually missing draft on a face that would never release.
claims.quote_verbatim: You have no draft angle here. Like, this is never going to inject from a mold
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: The mold designer gives the same kind of free design feedback a contract manufacturer gives on a board: thin walls, missing slope and unbuildable geometry, all identified before any steel is cut.
claims.quote_verbatim: if you could sit with a mold designer, they're gonna tell you like, that wall's too thin, this is a terrible design, this should be sloping
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: Choosing a stock container as the enclosure removed the need to produce any enclosure at all for a first product, and became a deliberate constraint rather than a compromise.
claims.quote_verbatim: it was really helpful because we didn't have to produce an enclosure
claims.speaker: Zach Dunham

claims.claim_text: Tooling can consume a crowdfunding raise outright: on one campaign the mold costs alone would have taken most of the roughly $170,000 raised.
claims.quote_verbatim: The mold costs alone would have eaten up most of their $170,000 they got or something
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Get Smart About Automation - Caducous Cyborg Concerns

claims.claim_text: Crowdfunding publishes an idea before the team has any way to build it, and campaigns are routinely run far too early by people who have no route to a molded part or a manufacturable board and then cannot afford the engineers to get one.
claims.quote_verbatim: they have no idea how to do injection molding or electronics design
claims.speaker: Bunnie Huang

claims.claim_text: Gate placement is a classic first-product failure: putting the injection points in the wrong position in the tool is the kind of mistake that surfaces only once parts come out.
claims.quote_verbatim: the injection mold points were at the wrong place in the mold
claims.episode_title: Shiny New Pebble with Eric Migicovsky

claims.claim_text: A mold designer's effectiveness came from sitting alongside the manufacturing engineer and understanding how the machine and the flow of the plastic constrain what the tool can be, then feeding that back into the design.
claims.quote_verbatim: the constraints of the injection molding machine really, and the way the plastic flows
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell

claims.claim_text: A part that cannot be made is not a design at all, which is why manufacturability is treated as part of the design rather than a downstream check.
claims.quote_verbatim: A design is only as good as, you know, its ability to be manufactured
claims.speaker: Aaed Musa

claims.claim_text: Ordinary molded consumer goods cost fractions of a penny per part, and the process is mature enough that additive manufacturing is unlikely to displace it at that end of the market.
claims.quote_verbatim: that thing costs fractions of a penny to make
claims.speaker: Spencer Wright

claims.claim_text: Choosing among thousands of molders resists rating systems, because a buyer who had a good project leaves five stars and a buyer who had a bad one simply walks away rather than damage a relationship they may need again.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's very little incentive for me to leave anything but a five star rating
claims.speaker: Spencer Wright

claims.claim_text: Toy-industry practice is to be physically present whenever a tool is opened, with trips batched around the run-up to the holiday season.
claims.quote_verbatim: Every time they're opening an injection molding tool, he's out there
claims.speaker: Scotty Allen

claims.claim_text: Staying on printed parts is defensible while the product is still changing, and the signal to move to tooling is capacity: printing caps how many units can be assembled in a month regardless of demand.
claims.quote_verbatim: there is still a max on how many I could put together in a month
claims.speaker: Jason Huggins

claims.claim_text: Taking a molded product to volume calls for a mechanical engineer with tooling experience in both molding and die casting, comfortable with tolerances and with working directly with contract manufacturers, which is a distinct hire from the board designer.
claims.quote_verbatim: doing injection molding, uh, like all our stuff is injection molded and, and doing all the tolerances and working with the CMs
claims.speaker: Brandon Gilles
claims.episode_title: Depth and AI with Brandon Gilles and Brian Weinstein

claims.claim_text: Standard chip encapsulation could not be adapted to leave a window for a display, so the product instead used a molded enclosure over the assembled board to get the shape they wanted.
claims.quote_verbatim: there's no way that we can sort of mask out a space for your OLED to shine through
claims.speaker: Marcus Schappi
claims.episode_title: An Interview with Marcus Schappi - Kit Ketch Kenophobia

claims.claim_text: Defence and consumer molding operate at incompatible scales, so a supplier tooled for military volumes cannot simply take commercial work to stay busy between contracts.
claims.quote_verbatim: someone's doing an injection molding for like a kid's toy in like the injection mold or for the military, like just the, the scale is completely off
claims.speaker: Chris Gammell
claims.episode_title: Psst...Hey buddy, wanna buy an Octopus?

ep325: the die-casting explanation is the guest answering; bundle labels the turn Chris Gammell. Attributed to David Kronstein by content.
